article.description: For most of the past year, "AI in construction" meant reading. Scan the spec. Flag the discrepancy. Summarize the submittal. Helpful, the way a very f

posts.content:
Quantity takeoff, material takeoff, cost estimate. They get used like they're interchangeable, and that's exactly how a project ends up with numbers nobody can explain later.

A quantity takeoff is just what the drawings show. A material takeoff adds in what you actually need to buy, waste and all. A cost estimate is what it all costs. Mix them up, and a small drawing change can force a full remeasure instead of a five minute fix.

How does your team keep these three straight? More on it here: https://lnkd.in/exTJkKZT

#Estimating #Construction

Before Shanen Aranmor, MS, CWI/CWE became a certified welding trainer, she was a therapist and later a college professor. Blacksmithing gave her an outlet. Welding gave her a calling.

She went on to become Miller Electric's first woman trainer. At one session, a man asked her to "go get the teacher." She wrote her name on the board and taught the class anyway.

Today she runs Weld Like a Girl, Welder Corps and Future Welding Inspectors, teaching students from age 5 to 88, including veterans and their families, how to build real skills with their hands.

Her message to every student: "People need to know that they're enough."

Read the full story on the Built Blog: https://lnkd.in/eYaGPNXs

Your takeoff isn't really done when you hit "finish." It's done when the drawings change and your numbers still hold up.

Most #takeoffs don't fail on day one. They fail three revisions later, when an addendum lands and the whole estimate needs a rebuild.

We dug into why that happens and what a revision-ready takeoff actually looks like: clean quantities kept separate from waste factors and pricing, markups you can see, layers organized by trade or phase, and measurements updated right at the source instead of copied and re-copied until nobody trusts the numbers.
